entries.title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
entries.abstract:
Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $\Omega(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task.
  Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.
entries.authors: Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Grigoris Velegkas, Felix Zhou

entries.title: Linking Rapid Learning to Compositional Structure in Neural Networks: Evidence from Additive Analogies in Meta-Learned Parameter Spaces
entries.abstract: Humans can learn rapidly from limited experience, while neural networks typically require extensive training. In this work, we investigate what properties of a neural network can enable it to learn rapidly. We study neural networks that have been optimized via meta-learning, a technique that exposes a network to many related functions to facilitate its subsequent learning of similar functions. Prior work has shown that these meta-learned networks can learn new functions rapidly, but how they do so remains unclear. To investigate their internal structure, we take inspiration from classic work demonstrating additive relationships among the learned vectors that neural networks use to represent words (e.g., "king" minus "man" plus "woman" approximates "queen"). Analogously, we look for additive relationships among a meta-learned network's "representations" of different functions; when a meta-learned network rapidly learns to implement a specific function, all of its adapted parameter values can be concatenated into a single vector that we treat as representing the function. We find that such parameter vectors can be added and subtracted according to symbolic relationships among the functions they represent, yielding new parameter vectors that successfully represent the functions predicted by the corresponding symbolic manipulations: the networks specified by these artificially recombined vectors actually implement the intended functions without any direct training on them. Our results suggest that meta-learning can tune a network's starting point to organize subsequent learning along systematic, functionally meaningful trajectories through the space of possible parameter vectors, providing a geometric basis for realizing inductive biases in neural networks.
entries.authors: Abigail L. Tenenbaum, R. Thomas McCoy

entries.title: Countable dynamical systems with a dense orbit
entries.abstract:
We study countable dynamical systems with a dense orbit. Given an infinite compact metric countable space $X$, we show that $\mathcal{DO}(X)$, the collection of continuous functions on $X$ to itself admitting a dense orbit, is always nonempty. We then classify the systems in $\mathcal{DO}(X)$ up to topological conjugacy in terms of the second Cantor--Bendixson derivative $X^{(2)}$: if $X^{(2)} = \emptyset$ then all systems in $\mathcal{DO}(X)$ are mutually conjugate, while if $X^{(2)} \neq \emptyset$ then $\mathcal{DO}(X)$ contains $2^{\aleph_0}$ pairwise nonconjugate systems. The proof of the latter relies on a gluing construction for countable dynamical systems with a dense orbit, which is of independent interest. We also show that $\mathcal{DO}(X)$ is nowhere dense in $C(X,X)$ with the compact-open topology.
  We also study the Ellis semigroup $E(X,f)$ of a countable dynamical system. We characterize, under the assumption that $|\omega(x,f)| = 1$ for each $x \in X^{(1)}$, when the nontrivial functions of $E(X,f)$ are continuous. In particular, for the family constructed on spaces with $|X^{(2)}| \geq 2$, every nontrivial function of the Ellis semigroup is discontinuous.
entries.authors: Jhon P\'erez-Remolina, Carlos Uzc\'ategui-Aylwin

entries.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
entries.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
entries.authors: Peiwen Li (Yale University), Harshit Verma (Yale University), Sophia Zhou (Yale University), Haiwen Wang (Yale University), Ngoc Bui (Yale University), Heng Chang (Tsinghua University), Fei Fei (Goodvision AI), David van Dijk (Yale University), Rex Ying (Yale University)

entries.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
entries.abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.
entries.authors: Ethan Lin, Akanksha Sarkar, Ziang Liu, Kristin Branson, Jennifer J. Sun

entries.title: A hyperbolic area proof of the Kahn-Lyubich Covering Lemma and its generalization
entries.abstract:
The Covering Lemma of J. Kahn and M. Lyubich is a fundamental analytic tool for controlling conformal moduli of annuli under branched coverings of finite degree. In the last several decades, it has played a crucial role in establishing rigidity of multicritical polynomial and rational maps. The classical proof uses the Near-Degenerate Regime as the main mechanism. In this short note, we prove this lemma using hyperbolic area and the Dirichlet energy. We also establish a version of the Covering Lemma for holomorphic maps of infinite degree.
  Our argument is inspired by recent applications of the hyperbolic area method to the study of wandering domains in rational and transcendental dynamics.
entries.authors: Kostiantyn Drach

entries.title: Internalizing Investment Mandates: A Neurosymbolic RL Approach to Portfolio Allocation
entries.abstract: Institutional portfolios operate under investment policy statements that specify asset allocation constraints, often conditioned on market regime information. Deep reinforcement learning has been shown to optimize financial performance but typically does not enforce rule compliance, making it unsuitable for real-world deployment. Existing neurosymbolic methods such as Probabilistic Logic Policy Gradient (PLPG) offer constraint-satisfying reinforcement learning (RL) via differentiable symbolic supervision but assume a finite, discrete action space. We present a PLPG-inspired continuous allocation method that estimates the probability that the policy's own executed action satisfies the investment mandate, using reparameterized Monte Carlo sampling, and adds it to the training objective. No post-hoc enforcement mechanism intercepts actions at inference time and compliance is learned by the agent. Audited directly on deterministic mean actions with no correction, the policy reduces violations of a six-rule regime-conditional mandate from 96-98% for unconstrained RL and 33.4% for a reward-penalty baseline to 4.8%, showing that a continuous-action neurosymbolic policy can substantially internalize a symbolic mandate.
entries.authors: Zeynep Y{\i}ld{\i}z, Satchit Chatterji, Ercan Atam, Erman Acar

entries.title: ArchSpace: Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing LLM Architecture Research
entries.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
entries.authors: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu, Yunkai Chai, Dehong Zheng, Yu Cheng, Tao Ji, ZhouHan Lin, Qi Zhang, Bowen Zhou

entries.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
entries.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
entries.authors: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li, Mike Lewis, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Luke Zettlemoyer, Lucas Beyer, Mengye Ren, Jakob Verbeek, Saining Xie, Hu Xu
